rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late-eluting compounds. The retention window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity experiments.

All pairs have resolution to spare, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed will reveal which critical pairs lose resolution as the gradient steepens.

Use an intermediate gradient duration to recover resolution in the central cluster while retaining most of the speed gain. This isolates slope effects and tests the trade-off between the resolution and time penalties.
Keep the promising gradient slope and test temperature selectivity on the sole under-resolved pair. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, leaving room to flatten the gradient if needed.

The central pair appears to have reversed elution order between 40 and 50 C; another 5 C may separate it sufficiently while keeping the run short. This smaller temperature step also limits the risk of merging the approaching earlier pair.

Slightly steepen the gradient at 55 C to improve the central pair now that its elution order has reversed, while further shortening the run. The earlier approaching pair will be monitored for any loss of baseline resolution.

Injection 6 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Slightly flattening its gradient tests whether the earlier critical pair gains separation while the central pair stays above 1.5 and the time penalty remains zero.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a modest increase in starting organic fraction for a faster method with improved resolution margins. This changes the gradient window and may shift the balance between the two critical pairs without making the first peak unretained.

Lengthen injection 8's gradient to recover separation of the earlier critical pair, while its central pair has some resolution margin. This may retain the maximum CRF with better minimum resolution than the current best method.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower gradient to improve the balance between the two critical pairs. Injection 9 suggests this may increase resolution margins while retaining a short enough run for maximum CRF.

Slightly flatten injection 10's gradient to raise the earlier critical pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the central pair's margin. The modest retention increase should still leave the time penalty at zero.

Flatten the gradient one more grid step to balance the two critical pairs near R = 1.7. The last peak is expected around 9.5 minutes, potentially preserving maximum CRF with greater resolution margin.

Trim the unused high-organic portion of injection 12 while keeping nearly the same gradient slope. Its last peak exited near 0.54 organic, so this endpoint should keep all peaks within the gradient and preserve maximum CRF.

Test a trimmed gradient with a slope between injections 9 and 12, aiming to retain baseline separation and zero time penalty. The 0.65 endpoint leaves ample organic-strength margin for the last compound to elute during the gradient.

With maximum CRF already secured, test whether 60 C offers a second high-resolution operating region. A longer gradient should help protect the approaching earlier pair while higher temperature separates the central pair and offsets some added retention time.

Return to 55 C and use a trimmed gradient with nearly the same slope as the maximum-scoring injection 9. This should preserve baseline separation with zero time penalty while avoiding the selectivity loss observed at 60 C.

Slightly steepen injection 16's gradient to shorten retention while balancing its two critical pairs more evenly. The last peak should still elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, with both critical resolutions above 1.5.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 17 to test a faster maximum-scoring method with more evenly balanced critical resolutions. The observed slope response predicts the earlier pair near R = 1.54 and the central pair near R = 1.60.

Maximum CRF is already secured at 55 C; test a lower-temperature selectivity region using the same gradient as injection 6. This will determine whether temperature-driven elution-order changes offer another fully resolved, short method.

Return to the proven 55 C region and interpolate the gradient slope between injections 12 and 13, where the two critical resolutions were nearly balanced. This should preserve maximum CRF with both critical pairs near R = 1.7.

Trim injection 6's unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope exactly. All peaks should elute during the gradient, retaining its maximum CRF and approximately 7.6-minute last-peak time.

Slightly steepen the balanced gradient from injection 20 to shorten retention while retaining resolution margins. The nearby results predict both critical pairs above 1.5 and a last-peak time near 9 minutes, preserving maximum CRF.

Refine between injections 20 and 22 with a slightly shorter programmed gradient and an intermediate slope. Both critical pairs should retain resolution margins above 1.5, with all compounds eluting during the gradient and no time penalty.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 20 to check the upper-retention edge of the maximum-CRF region. Both critical pairs should remain above 1.5, with the last peak expected near 9.6 minutes and no time penalty.

Test an untried, slightly shallower gradient than injection 24, with the last peak expected near 9.8 minutes. Both critical pairs should remain above R = 1.5, potentially preserving maximum CRF with a trimmed solvent window.
